content: Antipokhmelin is a Russian tablet designed to prevent or alleviate the adverse effects of alcohol consumption and hangovers. Its primary active ingredient is succinic acid, a compound also found in amber. In the United States and the United Kingdom, it is marketed under the name RU-21. The claims regarding its effectiveness are largely anecdotal, as no placebo-controlled, double-blind studies have been published in peer-reviewed scientific journals to substantiate these claims. RU-21 was developed by Professor Eugene Mayevski at the Institute of Theoretical and Experimental Biophysics, a division of the Russian Academy of Sciences, where the product also underwent clinical testing. Additional testing was conducted by the Russian Ministry of Public Health, which confirmed the product's effects on the body's ability to metabolize alcohol. An urban legend surrounding RU-21 attributes its development to the KGB. According to this legend, KGB operatives sought a chemical compound that would allow them to consume large amounts of alcohol with suspected Western intelligence agents, either in the Soviet Union or abroad, without becoming intoxicated. The idea was that the Western agents would become drunk and potentially divulge secrets, while the KGB agents, feigning intoxication, would remain fully lucid. While this strategy reportedly failed, the KGB agents discovered an unexpected side effect of the compound: its apparent ability to reduce hangover symptoms. Although there is some truth to this legend—specifically, that the KGB conducted alcohol-related experiments involving succinic acid, a key ingredient in RU-21—the KGB had no role in the product's commercialization. Following its successful launch in the United States, RU-21 quickly gained international distribution and became something of a cultural phenomenon. Despite the absence of articles in peer-reviewed journals, RU-21 has achieved recognition among consumers through word-of-mouth and endorsements from prominent publications such as GQ, Rolling Stone, and the New York Post. According to recent rumors, the brand is being acquired by a larger company that intends to market a new formula under the RU-21 name.
